name: Progressivism
summary: Progressivism seeks deliberate social improvement through democratic reform, wider effective freedom and a fairer distribution of opportunity and economic resources. Its defining accounts support public action to counter concentrated power while differing over institutional design, ownership and the role of religion. Contemporary self-definitions also emphasise sustainability and cooperation.
scope: The political reform tradition described by Thompson (s28), CAP’s defining intellectual and human-rights studies (s17, s16), the Encyclopedia of Religion and Society (s9), and Compass’s account of progressive politics (s27). These sources discuss historical American progressivism and its later development, alongside a British definition combining democracy, equality and sustainability; the name is not reduced to a present-day US caucus. Croly’s The Promise of American Life and Dewey’s The Public and Its Problems count only as the specific seminal/canonical works that s17 identifies. An organisation’s account of progressive principles is used as a definition, not as authority for its wider platform. Historical exclusions and religious contributions are not removed by definition; a general observation that the movement varies does not itself answer a statement.

notes: Later pass checked all statements, including candidates. Read the full CAP intellectual, human-rights and faith studies, Thompson’s scholarly pamphlet, Shalin’s article, Compass’s definition and the complete ThinkProgress article. Downloaded and searched Croly’s seminal book and Dewey’s named political text through the project Gutenberg tool and local corpus, across economy, government, society, world, liberty, culture, ecology, technology, means and globalism. The local reference library contains a Russell review of Dewey’s logic book, not an additional defining progressive political text. Public-office speech and vote corpora cover individual adherents, not the ideology’s own record; party-in-government measures are not treated as official-doctrine regimes. Original Wikipedia sources and the 1912 platform are retained for review history; no current answer rests on Wikipedia or a caucus programme. CAP article pages, Britannica, Oxford, Cambridge, Cairn, Paperity, Sage and Harvard Law Review pages returned HTTP 403; no refused page was retried. The accessible official CAP PDF copies were different copies of the works. GitHub searches found no full-report mirror. Routledge’s full entry is paywalled, so only its visible definition is used. The ThinkProgress article was read as a lead; its handbook excerpts do not license importing further unverified handbook claims. The validator rejected the ThinkProgress definition because its text says progressive rather than naming Progressivism twice; it is therefore not used for answers. Its related claims were checked against qualifying defining sources. Follow-up research concentrated on international affairs, nationalism, local versus central authority, religion, ecology and technology. Croly’s colonial-tutelage prescription is recorded against Compass’s opposed judgment as a split. His hypothetical discussion of an investigation into eugenic restrictions is documented in the nulling rationale rather than excluded as an embarrassing historical excess or converted into a settled policy. Modern sources and the specific canonical texts are distinguished in the rationales. The sources do not provide an ideology-wide position on newer technologies, specific emissions targets, nuclear power, indigenous autonomy or the many other remaining null questions.
